title: Scattering channels, stationary resolvents and time delay

items.title: Wave, scattering and channel operators
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal H_0,\mathcal H$ be separable complex Hilbert spaces, $H_0$ and $H$ self-adjoint operators on them, and $J:\mathcal H_0\to\mathcal H$ a bounded linear map. Write $E_{H_0}$ and $E_H$ for their spectral projection valued measures. The absolutely continuous subspace $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0)$ consists of vectors $u$ for which the scalar measure $B\mapsto\|E_{H_0}(B)u\|^2$ is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure; $P_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0)$ is its orthogonal projection. Define the two-space wave operators, when the pointwise strong limits exist on $\mathcal H_0$, by

$$\Omega_\pm(H,H_0;J):=\operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\pm\infty} e^{itH}J e^{-itH_0}P_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0),$$

where a strong limit means that for every $u\in\mathcal H_0$ the vector-valued expression converges in $\mathcal H$. The two signs are separate limits. When $J=I$ and $\mathcal H_0=\mathcal H$, write $\Omega_\pm(H,H_0)$. A wave operator is complete when its range is all of $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)$. When both wave operators exist and are isometries on $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0)$, the scattering operator on that subspace is

$$S(H,H_0;J):=\Omega_+^*\Omega_-.$$

When both are complete with common range $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)$, $S$ is unitary. For a fixed finite number $r\ge1$ of channels on an open energy interval $I\subset\mathbb R$, finite-channel data additionally consists of the standard space $\mathbb C^r$ and a matrix field $S:I\to U(r)$, where

$$U(r):=\{U\in M_r(\mathbb C):U^*U=UU^*=I_r\}.$$

Here $U^*$ is conjugate transpose, $\operatorname{tr}U=\sum_{j=1}^r U_{jj}$, and $\det U$ is the usual alternating determinant. The fixed channel number means that $I$ contains no channel threshold. This finite-channel data is an explicit on-shell input; the abstract wave-operator definition alone does not assert that a given pair has finite-dimensional energy fibers.
items.proof_route: Define the two-space strong limits on the free absolutely continuous subspace, completeness, scattering operator, and separate fixed finite-channel input.

references.title: D. R. Yafaev, Lectures on Scattering Theory, Lectures 1–2, especially Definitions 1.1–1.3 and equations (2.14)–(2.16)
references.locator: PDF pp.2–3 and 10–11: wave and scattering operators, completeness, spectral representation, stationary scattering matrix.

items.title: Continued resolvent matrix elements and resonance poles
items.design_state: Scaffolder-added local A-page prerequisite; complete statement and argument authored before its consumers.
items.statement:
Let $T$ be self-adjoint on a complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ whose inner product is linear in the first variable, use the resolvent convention $R_T(z)=(T-zI)^{-1}$, and let $X\subseteq\mathcal H$ be a specified vector subspace. For $f,h\in X$, the scalar resolvent matrix element is

$$r_{f,h}(z):=\langle R_T(z)f,h\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z>0.$$

Given an open real interval $I$, a point $E_0\in I$, and a disk $D$ centered at $E_0$, a local analytic continuation of these matrix elements through $E_0$ is a specified family of holomorphic functions $\widetilde r_{f,h}:D\to\mathbb C$ agreeing with $r_{f,h}$ on $D\cap\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, for the stated $f,h\in X$. A **meromorphic continuation** on $D$ is instead a specified family $\widetilde r_{f,h}$ agreeing with $r_{f,h}$ on $D\cap\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, holomorphic on $D$ except for isolated poles. At every crossing point where no pole occurs it is a regular analytic continuation on a smaller neighborhood. For such a meromorphic continuation, if $z_0\in D$ is nonreal and for some $f,h\in X$ the continued function satisfies

$$\widetilde r_{f,h}(z)=(z-z_0)^{-k}q(z)$$

on a punctured neighborhood of $z_0$, for an integer $k\ge1$ and a holomorphic $q$ with $q(z_0)\ne0$, then $z_0$ is a pole of order $k$ of that continued matrix element. Such a pole is called a resonance matrix-element pole for the specified pair $(T,X)$ and continuation. This definition asserts neither that a continuation exists nor that a pole is an eigenvalue of $T$; the continuation and the chosen test vectors are part of the data.
items.proof_route: Define local continuation, finite-order matrix-element poles, the chosen test space, and the non-eigenvalue caveat.

references.title: M. Gadella and G. Pronko, The Friedrichs Model and its Use in Resonance Phenomena, §1.1 and §2
references.locator: PDF pp.2–4: resonance through analytic continuation of resolvent matrix elements and the reduced resolvent in the Friedrichs model.

items.title: Explicit Gaussian continuation of a free resolvent matrix element
items.design_state: Scaffolder-added local A-page prerequisite; complete statement and argument authored before its consumers.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. On $\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3,dp;\mathbb C)$ with $\langle f,h\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f(p)\overline{h(p)}\,dp$, let $H_0=M_{|p|^2}$ on its maximal domain $\{f:|p|^2f\in L^2\}$, let $g(p)=\pi^{-3/4}e^{-|p|^2/2}$, and put

$$m(z):=\langle(H_0-zI)^{-1}g,g\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z>0.$$

This is a dimensionless model; no physical units are assigned to $p$ or $z$.

For $w\in\mathbb C$, define the entire function

$$\mathcal E(w):=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\int_{\Gamma_w}e^{-\zeta^2}\,d\zeta,\qquad \Gamma_w=\{w+t:t\ge0\},$$

where $\Gamma_w$ is the horizontal ray oriented from $w$ toward $+\infty+w$. For any $E_0>0$, take a disk $D$ centered at $E_0$ with $0\notin D$, and the holomorphic square root $k:D\to\mathbb C$ with $k(E_0)=\sqrt{E_0}>0$. Then $m$ has the local analytic continuation through $E_0$

$$m_{\mathrm{cont}}(z)=2+2i\sqrt\pi\,k(z)e^{-z}\mathcal E(-ik(z)),\qquad z\in D.$$
items.proof_route: Evaluate the normalized radial Gaussian resolvent integral, continue its complementary-error-function form through positive energy, and verify upper-half-plane agreement.

references.title: M. E. Taylor, Introduction to Analysis in Several Variables, §3.1
M. Gadella and G. Pronko, The Friedrichs Model and its Use in Resonance Phenomena, §2
references.locator: PDF pp.3–5: reduced resolvent, form-factor integral and conditional analytic continuation through the continuous spectrum.

items.strategy:
**Given:** [A1], the Hilbert space, multiplication operator, normalized vector $g$, scalar resolvent element, and the disk and branch data in the Statement.

1.1 By [F1], $H_0$ is self-adjoint and nonnegative. The Gaussian integral in [F2], applied in each coordinate and combined with Tonelli [F4], gives $\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-|p|^2}\,dp=\pi^{3/2}$, so $\|g\|=1$. Polar coordinates [F3] and the resolvent multiplier therefore give
$m(z)=\frac{4}{\sqrt\pi}\int_0^\infty\frac{r^2e^{-r^2}}{r^2-z}\,dr$
for $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. The denominator is nonzero on the integration ray, and the integral is locally uniformly dominated on the upper half-plane, so it defines the stated resolvent matrix element. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5]

1.2 For $\operatorname{Re}a>0$, put $I(a)=\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}(r^2+a^2)^{-1}\,dr$. When $a>0$ is real, the Laplace representation of $(r^2+a^2)^{-1}$ and Tonelli [F4] give $I(a)=\int_0^\infty e^{-a^2s}\int_0^\infty e^{-(1+s)r^2}\,dr\,ds=\frac{\sqrt\pi}{2}\int_0^\infty\frac{e^{-a^2s}}{\sqrt{1+s}}\,ds$ by [F2]. The substitutions $u=\sqrt{1+s}$ and $v=au$ then give $I(a)=\sqrt\pi e^{a^2}\int_1^\infty e^{-a^2u^2}\,du=\frac{\sqrt\pi e^{a^2}}a\int_a^\infty e^{-v^2}\,dv=\frac{\pi}{2a}e^{a^2}\mathcal E(a)$, using the horizontal-ray definition of $\mathcal E$ for real $a>0$. [F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 The function $I$ is holomorphic on $\operatorname{Re}a>0$: on a compact subset of that half-plane, the denominator $r^2+a^2$ is uniformly bounded away from zero for bounded $r$, while $|r^2+a^2|\ge r^2-|a|^2\ge3r^2/4$ for $r\ge2\max|a|$. These estimates dominate the integrand and its $a$-derivative by an integrable Gaussian times a polynomial, so [F5] justifies differentiation under the integral. Writing $\mathcal E(w)=\frac2{\sqrt\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-(w+t)^2}\,dt$, the integrand and its $w$-derivative on each compact set of $w$ are bounded by $C(1+t)e^{-t^2/4}$ after enlarging $C$, so [F5] also proves that $\mathcal E$ is entire. Thus both sides of the identity in step 1.2 are holomorphic on the connected half-plane $\operatorname{Re}a>0$; since they agree for every positive real $a$, [F6] proves the identity throughout that half-plane. [step 1.2, F5, F6, algebra]

3.1 For $\operatorname{Im}z>0$, choose the square root $a=\sqrt{-z}$ with $\operatorname{Re}a>0$. Since $r^2/(r^2-z)=1+z/(r^2-z)$, $m(z)=2+\frac{4z}{\sqrt\pi}I(a)$; substituting the identity from step 2.1 and $z=-a^2$ gives $m(z)=2-2\sqrt\pi\,a e^{-z}\mathcal E(a)$.
On $D\cap\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, the root $a$ equals $-ik(z)$: both square to $-z$, and $\operatorname{Re}(-ik(z))>0$. Substitution gives $m(z)=2+2i\sqrt\pi\,k(z)e^{-z}\mathcal E(-ik(z))$ there. The right hand side is holomorphic throughout $D$, so it is the required local continuation through $E_0$. [step 2.1, F2, F5, algebra] ∎

items.title: Compact-support short-range scattering closure
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let
$V\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ and suppose there is a compact set
$K\subset\mathbb R^3$ such that $V=0$ almost everywhere outside $K$.
Let $\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, and set
$H_0=-\Delta$ and $H=H_0+M_V$ on
$D(H_0)=D(H)=H^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$. Use

$$\widehat f(p)=(2\pi)^{-3/2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-ip\cdot x}f(x)\,dx,\qquad \Omega_\pm=\operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\pm\infty}e^{itH}e^{-itH_0}, \qquad S=\Omega_+^*\Omega_-.$$

Here $M_Vf=Vf$, and the strong limits act on every $f\in\mathcal H$. Then:

(a) The wave operators exist, are isometries, and satisfy

$$\operatorname{ran}\Omega_+=\operatorname{ran}\Omega_-=\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)=\mathcal H_{\mathrm c}(H), \qquad \mathcal H_{\mathrm{sc}}(H)=\{0\}.$$

For $u\in\mathcal H$, write $\mu_u(B)=\|E_H(B)u\|^2$. The subspace
$\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)$ consists of vectors with
$\mu_u\ll dE$; $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{sc}}(H)$ is the subspace with atomless
scalar spectral measures singular with respect to Lebesgue measure;
$\mathcal H_{\mathrm{pp}}(H)$ is the closed span of eigenspaces, and
$\mathcal H_{\mathrm c}(H)=\mathcal H_{\mathrm{pp}}(H)^\perp$. These are the
canonical spectral-type subspaces of the PVM.

(b) The scattering operator $S$ is unitary on $\mathcal H$ and commutes with $e^{-itH_0}$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$.

Use time in the corresponding $\hbar=1$ evolution convention and the
standard scaled Schrödinger normalization in which the kinetic
coefficient $\hbar^2/(2m)$ is set to $1$. When length is dimensional,
$E$ and $V$ then have units $L^{-2}$ and $k=\sqrt E$ has units
$L^{-1}$; the proof is an operator deduction in this normalization.

(c) Put $\mathfrak h=L^2(S^2,d\sigma)$, where $d\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$, and define the normalized free energy transform

$$(F_0f)(E,\omega)=\frac{E^{1/4}}{\sqrt2}\widehat f(\sqrt E\,\omega), \qquad F_0:\mathcal H\to L^2((0,\infty),dE;\mathfrak h).$$

Fix a bounded ball $B$ containing $K$. For $E>0$,
$k=\sqrt E$, define bounded maps $Z_0(E):L^2(B)\to\mathfrak h$ and
$Z_0(E)^*:\mathfrak h\to L^2(B)$ by

$$(Z_0(E)f)(\omega)=\frac{\sqrt k}{4\pi^{3/2}}\int_Be^{-ik\omega\cdot x}f(x)\,dx,\qquad (Z_0(E)^*a)(x)=\frac{\sqrt k}{4\pi^{3/2}}\int_{S^2}e^{ik\omega\cdot x}a(\omega)\,d\sigma(\omega).$$

Let $R_H(E+i0):L^2(B)\to L^2(B)$ be the operator-norm limit
$\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\mathbf1_B(H-(E+i\epsilon)I)^{-1}\mathbf1_B$;
existence and continuity for $E>0$ are part of the stated supplier input.
The products below are these bounded maps on $B$. Then $F_0$ is unitary and
there is a measurable unitary field $S_{\mathrm{stat}}(E)\in\mathcal B(\mathfrak h)$ such that

$$F_0SF_0^*=M_{S_{\mathrm{stat}}(E)},\qquad S_{\mathrm{stat}}(E)=I_{\mathfrak h}-2\pi i\,Z_0(E)\bigl[V-VR_H(E+i0)V\bigr]Z_0(E)^*, \quad E>0.$$

The formula uses only positive energies; it makes no claim at the threshold $E=0$, and no long-range Coulomb potential is included.
items.proof_route: Apply the exact compact-support completeness and stationary/dynamical suppliers under their stated Fourier, resolvent, sign, regularity, and positive-energy conventions.

references.title: D. R. Yafaev, Lectures on Scattering Theory, Lectures 1–2
references.locator: Lecture 1, Definitions 1.1–1.3; Lecture 2, §§2.1–2.2 and equations (2.14)–(2.16), PDF pp.2–3, 6–11.

references.title: B. Zwiebach, Quantum Physics III, Chapter 7: Scattering, MIT OpenCourseWare (Spring 2018)
references.locator: §§7.1 and 7.3, PDF pp.1–4 and 12–15: positive-energy finite-range scattering setup, outgoing Green function, and integral scattering equation; it does not prove operator-theoretic completeness.

items.strategy:
**Given:** [A1], [A2], [F1]–[F5], and the operators and conventions stated above.

1.1 The Fourier convention in [F1] is $\widehat f_{2\pi}(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}f(x)\,dx$; with $p=2\pi\xi$, its multiplier $4\pi^2|\xi|^2$ is exactly $|p|^2$, and the unitary momentum transform is $(2\pi)^{-3/2}\int e^{-ip\cdot x}f(x)\,dx$. Thus the $H_0$ and domain $H^2$ in [F2] agree with those in the Statement. Since the potential is the same real bounded compactly supported multiplication operator, [F1] also gives the self-adjoint realization required by [F2]. [A1, A2, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 By [F2], the two stated pointwise strong limits exist with the exact sign convention $e^{itH}e^{-itH_0}$, are isometries, and have the stated individual ranges. That same supplier proves the absent singular-continuous subspace; [F5] fixes the PVM meaning of these spectral subspaces. In the degenerate case $V=0$, the approximants are $e^{itH_0}e^{-itH_0}=I$, so $\Omega_\pm=I$ and $S=I$. By [F4], the supplier's scattering operator is exactly the $S$ defined in the Statement, so its unitarity and free-group commutation give (b). [F2, F4, F5, algebra]

1.3 The Fourier scaling and energy change of variables in [F3] use the same momentum transform and $d\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$ as in the Statement. Hence the local $F_0$, $Z_0(E)$, resolvent boundary value, and compact-region generalized adjoint agree term-for-term with [F3]; no independent normalization or sign change is introduced. [F3, algebra]

2.1 Applying [F3] with the identical $H_0,H,V$ now proves that $F_0$ is unitary, that $F_0SF_0^*$ is multiplication by $S_{\mathrm{stat}}(E)$, and that the displayed stationary formula is unitary for every $E>0$. The result is conditional on AC, CC and the compact-support model and makes no threshold or Coulomb assertion. This proves (a)–(c). [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3] ∎

items.title: Wigner–Smith matrix for differentiable finite channels
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement:
Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open energy interval with fixed finite channel number $r\ge1$, let $S:I\to U(r)$ be $C^1$ in the finite-channel convention of [[def-nrqmx-scattering-channel-data]], and let $\hbar>0$. Define

$$Q(E):=-i\hbar\,S(E)^*S'(E),\qquad E\in I.$$

Then $Q(E)$ is Hermitian and

$$\operatorname{tr}Q(E) =-i\hbar\,\frac{(\det S)'(E)}{\det S(E)} =-i\hbar\,\frac{d}{dE}\log\det S(E),$$

where the last expression means the logarithmic derivative $(\det S)'/\det S$, independent of a choice of logarithm branch. If the incoming and outgoing bases are changed by energy-independent unitary matrices $U_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $U_{\mathrm{out}}$, so that $S^\sharp=U_{\mathrm{out}}^*SU_{\mathrm{in}}$, then

$$Q^\sharp=U_{\mathrm{in}}^* Q U_{\mathrm{in}}.$$

If $E$ is measured in joules and $\hbar$ in joule-seconds, $Q$ has units of seconds. This is an algebraic scattering-matrix result; it does not by itself establish an operational arrival-time or dwell-time interpretation.
items.proof_route: Differentiate unitarity and the finite determinant; derive fixed-basis covariance and state the energy-dependent-basis limitation.

references.title: Christophe Texier, Wigner Time Delay and Related Concepts: Application to Transport in Coherent Conductors, §2.2.4
references.locator: PDF pp.3–4, equation (17): incoming and outgoing Wigner–Smith forms and Hermiticity; equation (19): trace and determinant phase sum rule.

references.title: Helmut Haberzettl and Ron Workman, Time-Delay in a Multi-Channel Formalism, §§II–III
references.locator: PDF pp.2–3, equations (3), (7)–(9): channel time-delay matrix, unitary diagonalization and trace in eigenphases; the paper flags a convention error propagated from Smith's original paper.

items.strategy:
**Given:** [F1], [F2] and the data in the Statement.

1.1 Differentiating $S(E)^*S(E)=I_r$ entrywise gives $S'(E)^*S(E)+S(E)^*S'(E)=0$. Thus $A:=S^*S'$ satisfies $A^*=-A$, and $Q^*=(-i\hbar A)^*=i\hbar A^*=-i\hbar A=Q$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Since $S$ is unitary, $S^{-1}=S^*$ and $\det S\ne0$. Multilinearity of the alternating determinant gives $\det(I_r+hA+o(h))=1+h\operatorname{tr}(A)+o(h)$ for $A=S(E)^{-1}S'(E)$: terms linear in $h$ are exactly the $r$ choices of one diagonal entry, while every nonidentity permutation or two off-diagonal factors contributes $o(h)$. Applying this to $S(E+h)=S(E)(I_r+hS(E)^{-1}S'(E)+o(h))$ yields $(\det S)'(E)=\det S(E)\operatorname{tr}(S(E)^{-1}S'(E))=\det S(E)\operatorname{tr}(S(E)^*S'(E))$. Multiplication by $-i\hbar/\det S(E)$ proves the trace formula. [step 1.1, F1, F2, algebra]

3.1 For constant unitary $U_{\mathrm{in}},U_{\mathrm{out}}$, differentiation gives $(S^\sharp)'=U_{\mathrm{out}}^*S'U_{\mathrm{in}}$, while $(S^\sharp)^*=U_{\mathrm{in}}^*S^*U_{\mathrm{out}}$. Therefore $(S^\sharp)^*(S^\sharp)'=U_{\mathrm{in}}^*S^*S'U_{\mathrm{in}}$, proving the stated conjugation rule. Energy-dependent basis changes introduce derivatives of the basis matrices, so they are not covered by this claim. [step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

items.title: Resonance poles in an analytic rank-one model
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H_0$ be a self-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ with inner product linear in its first variable, bounded below, let $g\in\mathcal H$, let $\lambda\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and put

$$P_gf=\langle f,g\rangle g,\qquad H_\lambda=H_0+\lambda P_g\quad\hbox{on }D(H_0),\qquad R_0(z)=(H_0-zI)^{-1}.$$

Adopt as an explicit conditional input the rank-one resolvent interface: $H_\lambda$ is self-adjoint, and whenever $z\in\rho(H_0)$ and $d(z):=1+\lambda m(z)\ne0$, where $m(z)=\langle R_0(z)g,g\rangle$, one has

$$(H_\lambda-zI)^{-1} =R_0(z)-\frac{\lambda R_0(z)P_gR_0(z)}{d(z)}.$$

Spectral variables use the energy unit of $H_0$. If $\|g\|$ is
dimensionless, $m(z)$ has inverse-energy units and $\lambda$ has energy
units; in general the coupling is chosen so that $\lambda m(z)$ is
dimensionless.

Let $E_\star\in\mathbb R$, take an open disk $D$ centered at $E_\star$, and let $E_\star$ lie in an open interval $I$ on which the spectral PVM $E_{H_0}(\cdot)$ of $H_0$ is absolutely continuous: $E_{H_0}(N)=0$ for every Lebesgue-null Borel set $N\subseteq I$. Suppose $m$ and, for specified test vectors $f,h$ in a subspace $X\subseteq\mathcal H$, the free matrix elements

$$\langle R_0(z)f,h\rangle,\qquad a_f(z):=\langle R_0(z)f,g\rangle,\qquad b_h(z):=\langle R_0(z)g,h\rangle$$

have holomorphic continuations through $E_\star$ to $D$. Suppose $d_{\mathrm{cont}}(z)=1+\lambda m_{\mathrm{cont}}(z)$ has a zero $z_0\in D$ with $\operatorname{Im}z_0<0$ of finite order $k\ge1$, meaning that on some neighborhood of $z_0$ one has $d_{\mathrm{cont}}(z)=(z-z_0)^k q(z)$ for a holomorphic function $q$ with $q(z_0)\ne0$, and suppose $a_f(z_0)b_h(z_0)\ne0$. Then the continued matrix element $\langle(H_\lambda-zI)^{-1}f,h\rangle$ has a resonance pole of order $k$. In the simple-zero case its residue is

$$-\frac{a_f(z_0)b_h(z_0)}{m_{\mathrm{cont}}'(z_0)}.$$

In particular, for the Gaussian model $H_0=M_{|p|^2}$, $g(p)=\pi^{-3/4}e^{-|p|^2/2}$, and $X=\operatorname{span}\{g\}$, take $E_\star>0$, an open disk $D$ centered at $E_\star$ with $0\notin D$, and the holomorphic square-root branch $k_D:D\to\mathbb C$ normalized by $k_D(E_\star)=\sqrt{E_\star}>0$. (The subscript distinguishes this branch from the zero order $k$.) The continuation in the Gaussian lemma with precisely these disk and branch data supplies $m_{\mathrm{cont}}$; every interval $I\subset(0,\infty)$ is absolutely continuous by the radial spectral measure formula. Every finite-order zero of $1+\lambda m_{\mathrm{cont}}$ in the lower half of such a disk gives a pole of the continued scalar element $\langle(H_\lambda-zI)^{-1}g,g\rangle$. These poles are not nonreal eigenvalues of the self-adjoint $H_\lambda$.
items.proof_route: Apply the exact rank-one identity conditionally, prove pole order and residue, verify Gaussian noncancellation on positive energy, and exclude nonreal eigenvalues.

references.title: M. Gadella and G. Pronko, The Friedrichs Model and its Use in Resonance Phenomena, §§1.1–2.1
references.locator: PDF pp.2–6: resolvent-matrix-element definition of a resonance, the rank-one reduced resolvent denominator and poles from zeros.

references.title: S. Albeverio and P. Kurasov, Singular Perturbations of Differential Operators: Solvable Schrödinger Type Operators, Chapter 1, §1.1.1
references.locator: Theorem 1.1.1 and its proof, printed pp.9–10: exact rank-one resolvent formula for a bounded perturbation of a possibly unbounded self-adjoint operator.

items.strategy:
**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F6], and the free matrix-element continuations in the Statement.

1.1 Fix $z$ with $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. Self-adjointness of $H_0$ puts $z$ in $\rho(H_0)$; self-adjointness of $H_\lambda$ in [A1] puts it in $\rho(H_\lambda)$. Also $d(z)\ne0$: if $d(z)=0$, then $g\ne0$, $u=R_0(z)g\ne0$, and $(H_\lambda-zI)u=g+\lambda\langle R_0(z)g,g\rangle g=0$, contradicting $z\in\rho(H_\lambda)$. Thus [A1] applies on the upper half-plane. [A1, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 Pairing the rank-one identity [A1] against $f,h$ and using the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\langle R_\lambda(z)f,h\rangle
=\langle R_0(z)f,h\rangle-\frac{\lambda\,a_f(z)b_h(z)}{d(z)}$.
Each numerator term has the holomorphic continuation assumed in the Statement, so the right side defines the corresponding meromorphic continuation on $D$. [A1, given, F1, algebra]

2.1 By the finite-order zero hypothesis, $d_{\mathrm{cont}}(z)=(z-z_0)^k q(z)$ near $z_0$, where $q$ is holomorphic and $q(z_0)\ne0$. The product $a_f b_h$ is holomorphic and nonzero at $z_0$, so its quotient by $d_{\mathrm{cont}}$ has a pole of order exactly $k$. The first term $\langle R_0(z)f,h\rangle_{\mathrm{cont}}$ is holomorphic and cannot cancel that pole. Thus the continued $H_\lambda$ matrix element has the asserted resonance pole. If $k=1$, its residue is $-\lambda a_f(z_0)b_h(z_0)/d'_{\mathrm{cont}}(z_0)=-a_f(z_0)b_h(z_0)/m'_{\mathrm{cont}}(z_0)$. [step 1.2, given, F1, algebra]

3.1 In the Gaussian model of [F2], choose a Borel representative of $|u|^2$ by [F6]. The PVM formula [F4] and polar integration [F5] then give, for every $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)$,
$\mu_u(B)=\int_{\{|p|^2\in B\}}|u(p)|^2\,dp
=\int_{B\cap(0,\infty)}\frac{\sqrt E}{2}
\int_{S^2}|u(\sqrt E\,\omega)|^2\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dE$.
The substitution $E=r^2$ gives $r^2\,dr=(\sqrt E/2)\,dE$. Thus $E_{H_0}(N)=0$ for every Lebesgue-null $N\subset(0,\infty)$, so any open $I\subset(0,\infty)$ meets the Statement's absolute-continuity condition. For $f=h=g$, one has $a_g=b_g=m_{\mathrm{cont}}$. At a zero of $1+\lambda m_{\mathrm{cont}}$, $m_{\mathrm{cont}}(z_0)=-1/\lambda\ne0$. Hence the noncancellation condition of step 2.1 holds at every finite-order zero, proving the stated Gaussian specialization. [F2, F4, F5, F6, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 If a nonzero vector $u\in D(H_\lambda)$ satisfied $H_\lambda u=z_0u$ with $\operatorname{Im}z_0<0$, self-adjointness in [A1] would make $\langle H_\lambda u,u\rangle$ real, but it equals $z_0\|u\|^2$, which is nonreal. This contradiction proves that the continued pole is not a nonreal eigenvalue. [A1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Cook existence is not completeness
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement: Every isometric wave operator has range equal to the full absolutely continuous subspace of the interacting Hamiltonian.
items.proof_route: Compute both wave limits for an exactly intertwining isometric embedding into a two-copy absolutely-continuous target, then compare its proper range with the full target subspace.

references.title: D. R. Yafaev, Lectures on Scattering Theory, Lecture 1, Definitions 1.1–1.2
references.locator: PDF p.3: existence/isometry of wave operators and the separate definition of completeness.

items.strategy:
**Given:** [A1], [A2], [F6]–[F8], the Hilbert spaces, operators, identification $J$, and unitary groups specified above.

1.1 By [F6], the Borel sigma-algebra on $(0,1)$ is countably generated, and by [F7] its measure is finite, hence sigma-finite. [F8] gives separability of $\mathcal H_0$; a direct sum of two separable spaces is separable because pairs from the product of countable dense subsets are countable and dense, so $\mathcal H$ is separable. Since $0<x<1$, $\|H_0f\|^2=\int_0^1x^2|f|^2\,d\beta\le\|f\|^2$, and $\langle H_0f,h\rangle=\langle f,H_0h\rangle$ for every $f,h\in\mathcal H_0$. Thus every $h$ belongs to $D(H_0^*)$, with $H_0^*h=H_0h$, proving self-adjointness by [F2]. The same componentwise pairing on the full domain $\mathcal H$ proves $H^*=H$. Its PVM is the multiplication family in [F3], so bounded Borel functional calculus gives $e^{itH_0}=M_{e^{itx}}=U_0(t)$ and $e^{itH}=U(t)$, consistently with [F4]. [A1, A2, F2, F3, F4, F6, F7, F8, given, algebra]

1.2 By [F3], every scalar spectral measure of $H_0$ is absolutely continuous, so $P_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0)=I$. Thus the projection in [F5] drops out. Using $Jf=(f,0)$, the two-space wave-operator approximants are exactly $U(t)J U_0(-t)f=(e^{itx}e^{-itx}f,0)=(f,0)$ for every $f\in\mathcal H_0$ and every real $t$. Since $HJ=JH_0$ and both generators are bounded, direct differentiation gives $\frac{d}{dt}(e^{itH}J e^{-itH_0}) =i e^{itH}(HJ-JH_0)e^{-itH_0}=0$. Thus the approximants are constant and both strong limits exist with $\Omega_\pm f=(f,0)$. Their norm equals $\|f\|$, so they are isometries. [F2, F3, F4, F5, given, algebra]

1.3 By [F3], every vector $f\oplus g\in\mathcal H$ has scalar spectral measure $B\longmapsto\int_{B\cap(0,1)}(|f(x)|^2+|g(x)|^2)\,dx$, which is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure. Therefore $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)=\mathcal H$. [F3, given, algebra]

2.1 The wave-operator range is $\mathcal H_0\oplus\{0\}$, which is a proper subspace of $\mathcal H$ because the constant function $1\in L^2((0,1))$ has norm one, so $0\oplus1$ is a nonzero vector outside the range. Hence the wave operators are isometric but not complete, refuting the statement. [F1, step 1.2, step 1.3] ∎

items.title: Elastic phase derivative
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement: Let $I$ be an open energy interval and let $\delta:I\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. The one-channel unitary matrix $S(E)=e^{2i\delta(E)}\in U(1)$ has Wigner–Smith matrix $Q(E)=2\hbar\,\delta'(E)$, which is real and has units of seconds when $E$ is measured in joules and $\hbar$ in joule-seconds. This algebraic quantity is not, without further model assumptions, an operational arrival-time measurement.
items.proof_route: Differentiate the one-channel phase and substitute it into the finite-channel Wigner–Smith definition.

references.title: Christophe Texier, Wigner Time Delay and Related Concepts: Application to Transport in Coherent Conductors, §2.2.1
references.locator: PDF p.3, equations (11)–(12): one-channel Wigner delay as the derivative of the scattering phase.

items.strategy:
**Given:** [F1] and the interval, differentiable phase, unitary matrix, and $\hbar>0$ in the Example.

1.1 Since $\delta(E)$ is real, $S(E)^*S(E)=e^{-2i\delta(E)}e^{2i\delta(E)}=1$; thus this is a one-channel unitary matrix on all of $I$. Differentiation gives $S'(E)=2i\delta'(E)e^{2i\delta(E)}$. [given, algebra]

2.1 Substitution into [F1] gives $Q(E)=-i\hbar e^{-2i\delta(E)}2i\delta'(E)e^{2i\delta(E)}=2\hbar\delta'(E)$, which is real. Since $\delta$ is dimensionless and $d\delta/dE$ has units $\mathrm J^{-1}$, $Q$ has units $\mathrm s$. No pointwise value of $Q$ is interpreted as a measured time. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
